The review describes a wheel-spin bonus in Cash Frenzy. The reviewer's complaint is that after the wheel visually stops on a large prize, the genie character moves the wheel to a different (lower) segment, so the player ends up with a much smaller payout (100 million with a 5x multiplier falling to 48 million). This is described as a deliberate, recurring design behavior rather than a bug, and the request for 'a player choice to keep or spin' is a suggestion for a non-existent feature, which is not codable under R12. The active mechanic being described is the game overriding the result the player saw: the wheel appears to land on a great prize and is then moved, which is a claim that the game manipulates the determination of an outcome and deceives the player about what they actually won. No real-money stake, purchase, or wager is mentioned, so Gambling is not triggered; the span is an outcome-manipulation claim, which matches Illusion of Control.

labels.rationale: The reviewer asserts that the wheel visibly stops on a great prize and the game then moves it to a lower-prize segment, i.e., the game manipulates the outcome after it is revealed, deceiving the player about what they won.

The reviewer describes three distinct experiences. First, a 30-second wait to connect to a match, which is matchmaking/queue time rather than a designed game gate, and the codebook explicitly excludes queue and matchmaking waits from Playing by Appointment. Second, rewards that 'seem' generous but are 'just for show,' which is a complaint about the value of rewards, not about how rewards are delivered, so Reward Mania does not apply. Third, difficulty obtaining weapon upgrades or perks, which leaves the player 'stuck battling to win' — this names the repeated activity (battling) that the player must perform to make progress. The closing line is a general evaluation that the game wastes the player's time, which by itself is not a mechanic.

parsed.analysis: The review describes ranked PvP in Clash Royale. The reviewer first complains that at high trophy counts (8k+) every opponent uses the same three cards (Mega Knight, PEKKA, Golem), which they find annoying to defend — this is a description of competing against other players in the game's ladder. The second and dominant complaint is that the game is pay to win: reaching higher ranks cannot be done through skill alone, and each update makes the pay-to-win nature worse and buffs cards players dislike. There is no mention of timers, currencies, ads, social invites, or collection mechanics. The two mechanics described are PvP competition and a paid advantage for progress/winning.

labels.rule_applied: definition / indicator: 'The game makes you compete against other players.'
labels.rationale: The span describes the player being matched against other players in a trophy-based ladder, which is direct player-versus-player competition structured by the game.

'not as many small and unnecessary tasks like celebrating' is a complaint about excess animations/tasks but describes no mechanism that blocks progress or prevents stopping, so it does not satisfy any label. labels.rationale: The suggestion presupposes an existing timer that gates a new life behind a wait; the reviewer is asking to shorten that wait, so the arbitrary life-regeneration schedule is the active mechanic (R12 codes the existing behavior the suggestion refers to).

parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing an in-game ad interstitial that traps them: the ad appears, has no close button, any tap redirects to the store, returning from the store leaves the game stuck on the ad's last frame, and the only way out is killing the app. Two design behaviours are being described. First, an advertisement the player is compelled to view because it cannot be dismissed through any intended control. Second, an interface that removes the opt-out entirely (no close mark) and routes every interaction toward the store, which is an obstruction of exit combined with direction toward a purchase destination.

labels.rationale: The ad cannot be dismissed by any in-game control and the only exit is killing the game, so the player is compelled to view it.

labels.rationale: The absence of any close control plus tap-anywhere-routes-to-store describes UI that blocks exit and funnels interaction to a purchase destination.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer states that uninstalling the game would wipe all of their progress and in-game purchases, and expresses reluctance to let that happen ('I really don't want that to happen'), which in turn makes them hesitant to spend more money. The actual request — that the developer add account-bound cloud saving — is a suggestion for a non-existent feature and is not codable under R12. But the review also asserts a currently present game behavior: progress and purchases are not saved to an account and are forfeited if the player leaves. That makes leaving costly because the player would abandon everything they have accumulated, and the reviewer explicitly lets this deter them from deleting the game. This is the invested-value arm of Easy to Get, Hard to Lose.

labels.label: P_EasyToGetHardToLose
labels.span: I know if I deleted the game I would lose everything my in-game purchases and my hard work I really don't want that to happen
labels.rule_applied: Invested (Endowed) Value indicator / canonical definition: accumulated investment raises the cost of leaving; exit entails forfeiting value the player already holds.
labels.rationale: The reviewer says deleting the game forfeits their purchases and hard work and that they don't want that, showing accumulated investment operating on their decision to stay and to hold back further spending — reluctant to abandon gains.

parsed.analysis: This is a wholly positive, promotional-style review. It praises graphics, storyline, strategic depth in building an empire, and real-time player-versus-player combat. There is no mention of payment, ads, timers, grinding, rewards, or any monetisation or retention mechanic. The only mechanic the text names that corresponds to a label is PvP combat: 'battling other players in real-time combat' directly describes the game placing players against each other. Phrases like 'kept me hooked from the start' and 'captivating storyline' are evaluative praise, not descriptions of a designed retention mechanism, so they do not lift to Easy to Get Hard to Lose. 'Depth of strategy required to build and expand my empire' is a general description of gameplay depth, not repetitive tasking, so it does not lift to Grinding. The positive tone does not suppress a label once the mechanic is named (R7).

labels.label: S_Competition
labels.span: the thrill of battling other players in real-time combat
labels.rule_applied: definition: 'Patterns that make players against each other in competition.' Indicator: 'The game makes you compete against other players.'
labels.rationale: The reviewer describes the game's PvP mechanic as battling other players in real-time, which places players against each other in competition; approval of the feature does not suppress the label under R7.

Second, they report difficulty obtaining dice and a losing run of no Shut downs or bank heists at max bet: this is a bad-luck streak, not an assertion that the game rigs outcomes, so it does not carry Illusion of Control. Third, 'Stickers are duplicates all the way' describes the sticker pack reward system giving repeated duplicate drops from a randomised pool. Finally, the login/network error is a technical fault and is not a deliberate design pattern, so it is not codable.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes a UI behaviour in the game: whenever the app is opened or the 1v1 lobby is entered, the interface automatically scrolls to and pre-selects the highest-stakes bet table affordable with the player's coins. The reviewer reads this as a deliberate "Dark UX" trick meant to provoke accidental taps, causing the player to lose accumulated coins and then be pressured into buying more with real money. The complaint is built around the default selection with no opt-out (they ask for a "Default Table Lock" and for the game to open on the lowest table by default). The review also establishes that the in-game coins are purchasable with real money ("forced to buy real ones"), i.e., an intermediate currency. There is no claim about rigged match outcomes or random reward delivery, so Illusion of Control and Gambling are not supported; the mechanics described are the interface's default-selection misdirection and the real-money purchase of the currency.

labels.rationale: The auto-scroll/auto-select is a default UI behaviour that steers the player into an unintended high-stakes action and causes accidental mis-clicks, which is exactly the interface directing attention/selection against the player's intent with no opt-out.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes trying the game once on a flight: it sat at 55% (presumably a loading or download progress bar) for five minutes, so they gave up and uninstalled. There is no description of any game mechanic, monetization, schedule, social pressure, or psychological manipulation. A stalled loading screen is a technical/performance failure, not a designed dark pattern. It does not match Fragmented Downloads, which requires obscuring the true storage requirement through a small advertised size, a download wall gating progress, or in-place asset download prompts; a slow or stuck progress bar alone describes a technical fault and falls under R11.

The review is a frustrated account of long-term play in Genshin Impact. The first complaint, that a 7-hour quest yields few primogems, is about reward size and value, not about the delivery mechanism, so it does not satisfy Reward Mania, and no real-money conversion is described, so Intermediate Currency does not apply. 'Exploration is debilitating' and the character-design criticism are evaluations with no mechanic named. The one mechanic the reviewer actually references is resin: in Genshin, resin is an energy resource that regenerates over time up to a hard cap and is consumed to claim rewards. The lament that 'there is no resin overflow system' only makes sense against that existing design — regeneration beyond the cap is wasted, so the player must log in and spend resin on the game's clock to avoid losing value. That is a time-based energy regeneration schedule imposing play on the game's schedule rather than the player's, i.e., Wait to Play / Playing by Appointment.

labels.rule_applied: Wait to Play (Hadan et al. 2024): 'Patterns that impose arbitrary wait times on players through in-game timers'; darkpattern.games: 'In-game timers that make you arbitrarily wait for something' — energy refilling over time to a cap is the canonical instance.
labels.rationale: The span implies the existing resin system regenerates over time to a fixed cap; without an overflow bank, the player must return on the game's schedule to spend resin before regeneration is forfeited, so the game's timer dictates when the player plays.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing sticker collection in MONOPOLY GO!. They say they enjoy the game but are frustrated with the sticker system: they keep getting duplicate stickers, and completing sticker sets is not possible unless they pay. Three mechanics sit in this short account. First, the player is engaged in completing sticker sets, and the review's frustration is that the sets cannot be finished, which is the collection-completion compulsion operating on the player. Second, the completion of those sets is gated behind payment, which is progress contingent on spending. Third, the duplicate drops come from a randomised reward pool: receiving repeats instead of missing stickers describes the delivery mechanism of the reward system, not merely its value.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer lists complaints about RAID: Shadow Legends. The statement that you 'almost have to buy stuff just to be able to keep playing' describes a pay wall where continued play depends on payment. The complaint that grinding returns 'practically nothing' names the repetitive activity required for progress and ties it to poor reward, which is Grinding. The lack of in-game guides is a usability complaint with no dark-pattern mechanism. Paying to unequip is a convenience/friction complaint not tied to progression or to real-money conversion, so it does not trigger a monetary label. 'Shards and gems are too hard to get' describes resource scarcity but never describes money being converted into those currencies, so Intermediate Currency does not apply.

parsed.analysis: The review lists six grievances about Candy Crush Soda Saga. Points 1 and 2 describe failed transactions: being charged 10 gold pieces for 5 extra moves when moves were still available, and paying for an unlimited-lives package that delivered the extras but not the lives. These read as erroneous charges or delivery faults rather than deliberate design mechanics, so under R11 they do not trigger labels. Point 3 describes timed bonuses that expire in real time while the player is offline: the bonus ticks away on the game's clock, so the player must play within the window to keep value, and waking up to find them gone is a loss imposed by the game's schedule. Point 4 states the player cannot win enough gold to keep playing without buying, which establishes both that gold is a currency purchasable with real money (Intermediate Currency) and that continued play depends on payment (Pay to Progress). Point 5 is only a price complaint. Point 6 says purchased packages should not be timed, confirming that bought content runs on a game timer, again a schedule operating on the player.

labels.rationale: The bonus value runs down on the game's clock whether or not the player is playing, forcing the player to play within the game-defined window or forfeit the reward.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes an album-collection system in Dice Dreams. They were two cards short of completing an album for a grand prize, so they bought a paid deal that promised new cards, but the deal delivered only duplicate cards. The album with a completion prize and a shortfall of the last cards is a collection-completion mechanic. The paid deal whose outcome (new vs. duplicate cards) is not guaranteed is a real-money stake in a chance-based reward delivery: the duplicates come from a randomised card pool. The reference to promoting the game through an external cash-reward app is out-of-game marketing and is not coded. 'Brain-rot' is an evaluation, not a mechanic. No currency conversion is described, so no Intermediate Currency. Nothing describes timers, schedules, or daily-login incentives.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing the live-service update cycle of Genshin Impact. Three distinct things appear. First, reward payouts are shrinking patch over patch, but that is phrased as a quantity/value complaint with no delivery mechanism described, so it does not instantiate Reward Mania's delivery-focused indicators. Second, the meta is described as shifting constantly, so that the player must pull for new characters to continue doing damage, which asserts that previously obtained characters have lost their damage value through new releases and that spending is becoming necessary to keep up. This is both Power Creep (devaluation of acquired characters through meta changes) and Pay to Win under Pay to Progress. Third, the phrase 'pull for new characters' names the gacha pull mechanic itself, which is a direct Reward Mania indicator; no monetary stake is described on the pulls, so Gambling is not assigned.

labels.rule_applied: Power Creep definition and boundary rule: value lost after acquisition through updates/new releases; subtle form where older characters no longer deal damage in current meta.
labels.rationale: The span asserts that constant meta changes make previously obtained characters unable to do damage, so the player must acquire new characters to stay competitive, i.e., acquired items lose value over time to drive new purchases.

labels.rationale: The reviewer explicitly names the game as becoming pay-to-win, where pulling new characters (funded by spending) is needed to deal damage, giving paying players the advantage needed for progress.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer's central complaints are (1) the game's store advertising misrepresents the actual product, which is a base-building game full of microtransaction menus, and (2) the game steers players into attacking one another while a large power gap separates paying from free players. The advertising complaint concerns third-party/store-listing marketing, which R13 puts outside the coded unit, and the mention of microtransaction menus is only a statement of abundance, not any friction-reducing purchase mechanism, so Easy to Purchase does not apply. The attack mechanic describes PvP competition between players, and the p2w/f2p gap describes paying players enjoying an advantage, which is the Pay to Win form of Pay to Progress. The anti-social reading is not warranted because the reviewer describes ordinary sanctioned player-versus-player combat, which the boundary rule assigns to Competition.

parsed.analysis: The review is about a Total Battle update that removed the open-silver PvP activity. The reviewer says two real things are happening now: meaningful growth requires spending money, and the removal of player-versus-player combat has made previously purchased growth pointless. A search was needed to pin down what 'open silver' refers to; it is the silver currency used in the game, and in context it names the open-world PvP looting activity that the update removed. Because the review explicitly says the PvP mode was taken away, the competition mechanic is no longer currently present and does not trigger S_Competition under R12. The paywall on growth is currently present, and the update's removal of PvP devalues money already spent on advancement, matching the devaluation-after-update test for Power Creep.
